text: # HOWTO: run and extend the clause-ledger lint Audience: any agent or human amending a clause ledger in this repo. ## Run it ```bash bash scripts/ledger-clauses-check.sh ``` Exit 0 = all ledgers well-formed. Exit 1 = violations printed to stderr, one per line, prefixed with `<product>/<clause-id>`. ## Common failures and fixes | Message | Fix | | -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `duplicate clause ID` | IDs are stable forever — renumber the NEW clause instead | | `missing Journey/Routes line` | add the `- **Journey:**` / `- **Routes:**` bullets to the clause body | | `landed clause evidence must cite a merged PR URL` | a landed claim without a merged PR is unverified: either downgrade the state to `drafted` or cite the PR that actually shipped it | ## State semantics (enforced shape, honest content) - `captured` — question recorded, no decision claimed. - `drafted` — keep/kill proposed with rationale + observable acceptance. - `landed` — acceptance verified against real routes; Evidence line cites the merged PR. The linter checks shape only. Whether a `landed` claim is TRUE is checked by comparing the cited route against reality — do that in review. ## Extending Add product-agnostic rules in `ledger-clauses-check.py` (stdlib only, no deps). Per-product policy goes in that product's clauses.md prose, never in the linter.

Replace each comment with real --> <!-- content (each TODO line is its own self-contained comment). --> # Design system: product-ui-docs ## Atomic design breakdown This repo owns no UI primitives of its own — it is a documentation product. Its 'atoms' are the document units: the **journey row** (trigger → outcome → screens), the **clause** (stable ID, lifecycle state, outcome, journey linkage, routes, acceptance, evidence), and the **disposition tally**. Molecules are the per-product ledgers (journeys.md + clauses.md); the organism is a complete product record; the template directory is the page tier. Where a future UI is needed (docs-viewer chrome), it consumes gyrum canon components rather than defining any. ## Hexagonal architecture The domain core is the clause model: stable ID, single lifecycle state from {captured, drafted, landed}, journey linkage, route-level acceptance, and merged-PR evidence for landed clauses. The driving port is the markdown documents humans and agents edit; the driven port is `scripts/ledger-clauses-check.py`, which reads the ledgers and fails on shape violations. No runtime services sit behind these ports by design — enforcement stays a PR-time lint until clause governance earns automation. ## Developer specifics Stack: plain markdown + one Python 3 stdlib script; no build step. Directories follow the scaffold: docs/products/<product>/ holds journeys.md + clauses.md per surface. Naming: clause IDs CL-<n> stable forever; states lowercase enum. Testing: `bash scripts/ledger-clauses-check.sh` is the gate (also wired as the golden-path check). Gates this repo declares in repo-type.yaml: standard profile with orientation-drift required; deployment contract is merge-only (deployable:false) because no image ships here.

--- title: product-ui-docs — docs guide status: living document last-updated: 2026-08-22 --- # product-ui-docs — docs guide > **This is a living document.** It is this repo's chapter in the > Fleet Book (warp#6279): the newcomer onboarding plus a reference > pointer into the rest of the docs. Distinct from the README (the > router — where to go). Refresh it whenever the shape of product-ui-docs > changes enough that a newcomer's mental model would be wrong. ## Onboarding — start here This repo is the **product-UI ledger** for Gyrum surfaces: the recorded argument for which screens exist and why. Canon owns the design-system vocabulary; this repo owns the per-product decisions — journeys, screen inventory, and a clause ledger where every keep/kill decision carries an enforced lifecycle (`captured → drafted → landed`). The one thing to understand before anything else: **a clause is not done until it points at evidence** — for `landed`, a merged PR URL. A proposal without evidence is opinion, and this repo's whole job is to keep opinion from masquerading as shipped product. Prove your checkout works: ```bash bash scripts/ledger-clauses-check.sh ``` To make a trivial change (e.g. flip a clause state after its PR merges): edit `docs/products//clauses.md`, run the check above, then go through the normal branch → review → merge flow. ## How it fits together No component diagram: this repo is documentation plus one lint script. The moving parts are the documents and their relationships: ```mermaid flowchart LR J[journeys.md
per product] --> C[clauses.md
keep/kill record] T[template/new-product.md] -. copied at birth .-> J M[method.md
validated process] -. governs .-> C L[ledger-clauses-check.py] -- lints --> C ``` - `docs/method.md` — the journey-first process, validated by the real ops.gyrum.ai reduction. - `docs/products//journeys.md` — what operators do, weighted, with evidence sources and admitted gaps. - `docs/products//clauses.md` — every surface decision as a clause; PRs cite clauses; landing requires merged-PR evidence. - `docs/template/new-product.md` — copy at birth for new products. ## How we got here | When | What changed | Why / reference | | ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | | 2026-08-21 | ops.gyrum.ai reduction EPIC raised (journey-first, not crawl-and-fix) | warp#14685 | | 2026-08-22 | Journeys + IA contract landed in ai-frontend | ai-frontend PR #1197 / warp#14686 | | 2026-08-22 | Reduced rail shipped (6 sections/22 seats, dupes killed) | ai-frontend PR #1200 / warp#14687 | | 2026-08-22 | This repo created + seeded: method, journeys, 12-clause ledger | warp#14690 | ## Reference — where to find everything | I need to… | Go to | | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | understand what this repo is | [README.md](../README.md) | | run the validated reduction process | [docs/method.md](method.md) | | see the ops.gyrum.ai journeys | [docs/products/ops.gyrum.ai/journeys.md](products/ops.gyrum.ai/journeys.md) | | read or amend a keep/kill decision | [docs/products/ops.gyrum.ai/clauses.md](products/ops.gyrum.ai/clauses.md) | | start documentation for a NEW product | [docs/template/new-product.md](template/new-product.md) | | lint the ledgers | `bash scripts/ledger-clauses-check.sh` | | see the design-system vocabulary this complements | https://canon.gyrum.ai |

Do not hand-edit; edit the devtools template and re-sync. --> # Devtools — full command reference, mechanics & rule rationale Companion to the **Devtools** section in `CLAUDE.md`. Read the relevant part when a trigger fires (a `gyrum-*` command's full flags/exit-codes, an always-on background mechanism's cadence/tunables, or the *Why* + mechanics behind a STRICT rule). The imperatives are in `CLAUDE.md`; the long-form command tables, the background-mechanism reference, and every rule's justification live here. ## Command reference (full) Gyrum devtools are installed at `~/.gyrum/devtools/` and exposed on PATH via `~/.local/bin/gyrum-*`. Prefer these over hand-rolling — they own the workflow contract (hooks, review gates, finding journal, worktree isolation). | Command | When to use | |---|---| | `gyrum-start-work <name>` | Start a feature: auto-isolates into a fresh sibling clone, creates branch + draft PR. `--in-place` to skip isolation. Final stdout line is `WORKTREE: <abs-path>` (or `WORKTREE-IN-PLACE: <repo-root>`) — non-interactive callers `cd` to that path before the next command. | <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> | `gyrum-workspace <name>` | Spawn a parallel sibling clone for spike/experiment work (`~/work/<name>`). Allocates a fresh TCP port from `~/.gyrum/workspaces.json`; emits `run-dev.sh` when the repo declares `server_command` in `.gyrum/workspace.yml`. | | `gyrum-complete-pr` | Finish a feature: pre-PR checks, 3-persona AI review, merge. | | `gyrum-review-pr` | Local 3-persona review on the current branch. | | `gyrum-review-remote <owner/repo#N>` | Review any PR in a fresh clone, no working-tree disturbance. | | `gyrum-followup-proposals --dry-run ...` | End-of-work follow-up substrate (warp#2968). Direct route renders/ files concrete scoped tickets only after a duplicate-search query; architecture-vote route records disputed or high-blast-radius proposals without creating implementation work. | | `gyrum-implement <spec>` | Scaffold + implement a pipeline step end-to-end. | | `gyrum-continue` | Resume an interrupted `/loop` or `gyrum-implement`. | | `gyrum-record-finding` | Log a cross-agent finding to `~/.gyrum/findings/findings.jsonl`. | | `gyrum-create-repo <name>` | Bootstrap a new gyrum-shaped repo (CI, branch protection, bots). | | `gyrum-setup` | (Re-)install hooks + aliases + this CLAUDE.md section. | <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> | `gyrum-bind-memory` | Symlink `~/.claude/projects/-<slug>/memory/` → `<repo>/.claude/memory/` so durable Claude memory lives in git (ADR-126 / warp#1004). Idempotent; run by `gyrum-setup`. | <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> | `gyrum-validate-playbook <file.yaml>` | Validate a playbook against ADR-067 schema + ADR-068 target rules before runtime. | | `gyrum-validate-structure <path>` | Shared structural validator for playbooks, pipeline/block YAML, and pipeline-step source — execution-plane, entrypoint, dry-run/approval, direct-prod-mutation policy. | | `gyrum-create-playbook <kind> <id>` | Scaffold a validator-clean playbook (onboarding / release_flow / service_runbook / journey / experiment / incident_response). | <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> | `gyrum-pre-flight` | Forced agent attestation before `gyrum-review-pr` (warp#1387). Prints a 3-digit pin + 7-item checklist; reads marked+pinned reply on stdin; appends to findings.jsonl; exec's `gyrum-review-pr`. Use after >15min autonomous work. | <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> | `gyrum-recover` | After non-zero `gyrum-review-pr` exit: read `./gyrum-review-findings.json` and print a markdown re-pass message naming the canonical rule, evidence, fix-hint, and override criteria for each failed gate. Pipe into the continuation message. | | `gyrum-brief --ticket warp#NNNN [--persona name] [--out path]` | Substrate-driven dispatch-brief generator. Pulls the ticket, parent epic's `docs[]`, the canonical gate attestation, persona recommendation, and an open-PR collision check; emits templated markdown (byte-identical when input is identical). Replaces ~150-line hand-rolled briefs. | | `gyrum-warp <ticket-id>` | One-shot ticket-to-merge verb (warp#2575). Delegates to `gyrum-start-work` for claim + worktree + draft-PR, renders a brief, spawns headless `claude -p`. `gyrum-warp --doctor` walks every prereq in one pass. | | `gyrum-warp search "<keywords>"` | Search Warp tickets before filing or claiming structural work; use repo names, paths, error text, feature names, or operator phrases to find related tickets to cross-link. | | `gyrum-warp preview <id-or-warp#NNN>` | Read a ticket without claiming it. Use to inspect candidate cross-links before adding `depends_on`, `blocked_by`, `context_links`, or `parent:warp-NNN`. | | `gyrum-verify-shipped warp#NNN [--json] [--require-terminal] [--allow-mention-only]` | Verify the cited closing PR merge separately from Warp Done (warp#2915, warp#19400). Default exit 0 means source merged: `SHIPPED` only when Warp is Done, otherwise `SOURCE-MERGED` with delivery pending. `--require-terminal` returns exit 5 until Warp is Done and requires an exact merge SHA before terminal success. Exit 1=cited PR unmerged, 2=no PR cited, 3=cancelled/blocked, 4=API error (including absent Warp status or missing SHA in terminal mode). JSON includes `ticket_status`, `merge_sha` (null when GitHub omits it), `delivery_state`, and `source_merged`. Strict close-verb matching remains the default (warp#2997); `--allow-mention-only` opts into legacy permissive matching. | | `gyrum-dispatch-check warp#NNN [--json] [--skip-already-shipped "<reason ≥ 20 chars>"]` | Orchestrator-side canonical-actionability and freshness check BEFORE `Agent(...)` dispatch (warp#3710, warp#16361). Sister to `gyrum-verify-shipped` (which fires at completion). Validates Warp's canonical actionability before GitHub lookups, then runs FOUR freshness queries — ticket status, merged-PR close-verb, open-PR close-verb, recent main commit reference. Exit codes: 0=dispatch-ok, 1=already-shipped, 2=in-progress (open PR or live claim), 3=terminal (done/cancelled/blocked), 4=recent-main-commit, 5=bypass-honoured (audited freshness refusal only), 6=usage/API error, 7=canonical non-actionable. Exit 7 cannot be bypassed; when a Ready canonical refusal also has a higher-priority live-claim verdict, the legacy shipment override remains ineligible and cannot produce exit 5. | <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> | `gyrum-fleet <subcommand>` | Unified AWS-style supervisor CLI (warp#3065): `status` / `scale` / `scale-plan <host>` / `pause @label` / `resume @label` / `stop @label` / `start @label` / `logs @label` / `kills` / `reserve <ticket> @label` / `unreserve <ticket>` / `claim-state <ticket>` / `containers` / `hosts` / `register-runner <name> <ip> [--count N]` / `runner-reset <name>` (warp#3175) / `host audit <alias> [--format=json] [--no-cache]` (warp#3166) / `host-info <alias> [--json]` (warp#7862). Replaces the SSH + systemctl + warp-API + docker + ansible choreography per fleet op with one verb per intent. `scale-plan` (warp#3168) is read-only pre-flight: emits a structural change-list (dispatch edits, stagger edits, host_enable rows, backend collisions) BEFORE you execute. `host audit` (warp#3166) is read-only single-host inspection: five sections (system + supervisor slot matrix + Claude OAuth credential layout + docker daemon state + last 5 systemd events per slot) cached at `~/.gyrum/fleet-audit/<alias>.json` for 30s; output schema at `schemas/host-audit.schema.json`; alias resolution via `dark-factory/infrastructure/server-ids.json` plus the `spare` LAN nick. Reads inventory from `~/.gyrum/devtools/etc/fleet-hosts.yml` (template: `templates/fleet-hosts.yml.example`); reservations require an admin token at `~/.config/gyrum/warp-admin.token`; runner-registration reads `dark-factory/infrastructure/server-ids.json`. `host-info` (warp#7862) is read-only "what serves on that box" in one ssh round-trip: containers (names+ports), :80/:443 listener owner, caddy/nginx/docker service states, Caddyfile `import sites/*.caddy` + `sites/` listing, `/opt` dirs, and a derived `proxy_mode` verdict (`edge-container`/`host-caddy`/`nginx`/`none`/`unknown` — the docker-exec-caddy vs systemctl-reload deploy fork); alias resolution from the CANONICAL `dark-factory/ansible/inventory.ini`; per-probe graceful degradation (missing docker = reported fact, not a crash). Operator quick-ref: `docs/runbooks/fleet-operator-quickref.md`; runner-registration runbook: `docs/runbooks/gyrum-fleet-register-runner.md`. | | `gyrum-help` | Print the up-to-date command list. | ## Background mechanisms (always-on, structural) <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> Deterministic shell loops / hooks / shims that fire when `gyrum-start-work` spawns a worktree. None calls an LLM. Full reference + tunables in devtools' `README.md`. | Mechanism | Cadence | What it does | |---|---|---| <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> | `lib/wip-checkpoint.sh` | every 600s | force-with-lease pushes a `WIP checkpoint <epoch> [skip ci]` commit on your feature branch. Refuses protected branches (warp#1986). | <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> | `lib/heartbeat.sh` | every 4 min | POSTs `/api/v1/items/<id>/heartbeat` to keep your Warp lease alive. | | `gyrum-deployed-sync` | every 5 min (systemd user timer) | fast-forwards tracked fleet checkouts to `origin/main`. | | `gyrum-service-version-drift` | every 30 min (systemd user timer) | hits each long-running service's `/api/version` badge and reports any whose running build SHA lags `origin/main` (binary deploy-lag, merged≠live), filing a deduped warp alert. Read-only — NEVER redeploys (warp#8860 detector, scheduled by warp#9328). | | `lib/agent-guard/{git,mv,rm,cp}` | per-call in agent shells | refuses sub-agent mutations to `~/work/` paths with exit 2. No-op for operator shells. | | `.githooks/pre-push` + `.githooks/commit-msg` | per push / commit | structural-checks gate. `--no-verify` is an audited bypass — operator authorisation only. | ## Rule rationale — the *Why* + mechanics behind each STRICT rule These rules are LOAD-BEARING. Persona-PAT rubber-stamping cannot reproduce the contracts devtools enforce. The "simpler-looking" alternative bypasses every gate. AI agents in particular: do not pick the simpler-looking path — it bypasses every gate. ### Merge path — review-pr → complete-pr, never `gh pr merge` `gh pr merge` directly bypasses the whole contract: `gyrum-review-pr` then `gyrum-complete-pr` from the feature branch verify the review pass, run structural checks, merge with the right strategy, and tag the version — none of which `gh pr merge` does. POSTing to `/pulls/:n/reviews` with a persona PAT and prose you wrote yourself bypasses the 3-persona AI review, replacing reviewer judgement with persona-themed prose. `gh pr merge --squash` is wrong because the convention is `--merge` so per-commit history is preserved (each commit independently testable and revertable); `gyrum-complete-pr` handles the strategy. ### `--no-verify` / `--admin` — audited bypass, never a workflow step Hook bypass on push and admin override on merge are emergency tools, not workflow steps; both need explicit written operator authorisation for the specific PR. Specifically for diff-size: warp#3100 Path-A atomic canon-author PRs (canon-manifest delta + matching Lit+adapter+tests+storybook trio for each added primitive, all paths on the Path-A allowlist) auto-skip the diff-size gate via `lib/review-checks.sh::_is_path_a_canon_atomic`, with one audited row per PR appended to `~/.gyrum/admin-overrides.log` (warp#3702). Do NOT reach for `--admin` on a legitimate Path-A ship — the gate already exempts it; reaching anyway re-introduces the warp#3100-vs-admin-no-bypass rule conflict the auto-skip exists to dissolve. ### `--ignore-failing-checks` — never to silence a real broken test (warp#3107) `gyrum-complete-pr` refuses to enrol auto-merge when `statusCheckRollup` contains any FAILURE conclusion — sister-shape to warp#3009's DIRTY refusal. The right path is the unblocker ticket workflow: `gyrum-warp add` a ticket for the failing test, `gyrum-warp block <current> --reason 'blocked-by:warp#NNN'`, return when the unblocker ships. The audited override exists ONLY for the case where the failing check is legitimately unrelated to this PR's scope AND an unblocker is already filed. ### Never `--blocked-by` an approved ticket; CI-infra waits are comments (warp#20986) Every persona approval carries a digest of the ticket it reviewed, and `gyrum-complete-pr` and the merge train count an approval only while that digest still recomputes. The digest signs the ticket's content (title, description, priority, tags, `blocked_by`, `depends_on` and the rest of `persona_review_evidence_canonical_ticket`) but not `status` or `blocked_reason`. A reason-only `gyrum-warp block` is therefore safe, while linking a blocker after review voids every approval on the PR. `gyrum-warp unblock` never clears `blocked_by`, so the void outlives the wait. warp#20986 traced 14 voided approvals to CI-infra blockers linked 30-60 minutes after approval. - **CI-infra wait** (dead runner, sandbox EPERM, rc=75 infra kill): not a blocker. Keep the claim, leave a ticket comment (`POST /api/v1/items/<id>/comments` with `{"body": "…"}`; there is no `gyrum-warp comment` verb yet), and re-run the checks once the infra recovers. - **Real broken test on main**: file the unblocker, then `gyrum-warp block <id> --reason "waiting on warp#NNN"`. The reason carries the link; `--blocked-by` would void the approvals. - **The guard**: `gyrum-warp block --blocked-by` exits 3 when an open PR linked to the ticket holds an APPROVED review carrying a persona evidence marker, and fails closed when it cannot check. It derives "signed" from the digest's own canonical ticket, so it stops refusing by itself if `blocked_by` ever leaves the signed set. Audited override: `--skip-signed-approval-guard "<reason ≥ 20 chars>"` (logged to `~/.gyrum/admin-overrides.log`). `gyrum-warp update --blocked-by` is not guarded yet; the rule applies to it all the same. ### `gyrum-review-pr` before opening — structural gate It gates structural checks (build, test, coverage, complexity, file length, gosec, staticcheck) that the persona review alone does not. Local review IS the review — there is no external review step. ### `gyrum-pre-flight` after >15 min autonomous work (warp#1387) The 3-digit pin is the structural delta vs documentary "remember the gates" prose; typing the pin is proof of read; the auto-appended findings line is the audit trail that makes "you said you did X, the diff shows you didn't" retrospectively answerable. Bypassing the wrapper is the same shape of lie as bypassing a gate. ### `gyrum-recover` on non-zero `gyrum-review-pr` exit It reads the structured review-findings JSON contract and prints a canonical re-pass message naming the rule body, evidence, fix-hint, and override criteria for each failed gate. Cuts the diagnose step from "parse stderr and back-translate to which rule" to "read structured rule references" — the agent fixes against the canonical rule, not the symptom. Pipe into the continuation message. ### `gyrum-complete-pr` immediately after SUCCESS (warp#1342) There is NO external review step — local review IS the review. The script's FINAL stdout line is a literal directive token (`READY-TO-MERGE — call gyrum-complete-pr` / `REVIEW-FAILED — fix findings then re-run gyrum-review-pr`); swarm agents pattern-match on it. Do not exit waiting for an async/external verdict; the verdict has already been printed — agents stalled holding orphan heartbeat leases on warp#1311 / warp#1330 by misreading local review as advisory. ### Follow-up proposals at wrap-up (warp#2968) Use `gyrum-followup-proposals --dry-run` before filing anything. Direct follow-up tickets require a duplicate-search query, concrete scope, and a `--pattern` precedent; disputed, cross-system, policy-changing, or high-blast-radius proposals go through `--route architecture-vote` so agent positions are preserved before implementation tickets exist. ### `AGENT-TERMINAL` vs `ENROLLED-NOT-YET-MERGED` (warp#3362) `AGENT-TERMINAL — merged` (or `— auto-merge enrolled` under the audited `--accept-enrollment-as-terminal "<reason ≥ 20 chars>"` legacy override) means the PR is genuinely merged (mergedAt non-null) — exit immediately, do NOT poll. `ENROLLED-NOT-YET-MERGED — BLOCKED: <named-blocker>` / `— TIMEOUT: <state-summary>` / `— POLL_DISABLED` means auto-merge enrolled but GitHub has not landed it yet — the caller MUST `gh pr view <N> --json mergedAt,mergeStateStatus,statusCheckRollup` to verify, then either wait (with a larger `GYRUM_AUTO_MERGE_WATCH_MINUTES`), file an unblocker ticket, or escalate. Reporting `AGENT-TERMINAL — merged` when the script emitted `ENROLLED-NOT-YET-MERGED` is the warp#3071 / warp#3060 false-claim regression the truth gate exists to prevent. `AUTO-MERGE-PENDING — enrolled, checks still running; re-run gyrum-complete-pr after merge` (rc=0, warp#13151) is the default bounded merge-wait outcome: complete-pr waited `GYRUM_COMPLETE_MERGE_WAIT_SECS` (90s default), verified the enrolled auto-merge is merely PENDING — PR still OPEN, no failed checks — and exited 0 instead of blocking the foreground through the whole CI duration. It is NOT a merge claim: re-run `gyrum-complete-pr` once the merge lands (the idempotent warp#12394 tail then completes in seconds) or poll `mergedAt` yourself. A FAILED merge (conflict / red required check / closed-without-merge) never emits this — those exit non-zero with the failure surfaced. `gyrum-complete-pr --tail` restores the pre-warp#13151 wait-through-CI shape when an in-session watch is genuinely wanted. ### Never trust an AGENT-TERMINAL claim from a non-clean sub-agent exit (warp#3144) The `gyrum-warp` dispatch wrapper classifies the spawn's actual exit reason (`clean_exit` / `watchdog_killed` / `timeout` / `rate_limited` / `crashed`) and refuses to forward an AGENT-TERMINAL-claiming report on any non-clean exit — rewriting the report to a `WATCHDOG-KILLED — orchestrator MUST verify via gh pr view <N>` directive and exiting non-zero. Sister to warp#3361 (persona-review-truth-gate at review-pr layer) and warp#3362 (post-enroll merge-watcher truth gate at complete-pr layer); together the three gates close the dispatch → review → complete loop against false-positive shipped claims. On any WATCHDOG-KILLED output, the orchestrator MUST `gh pr view <N> --json mergedAt,state,mergeStateStatus,statusCheckRollup` before treating the ticket as shipped. ### Fix pre-push hook failures at the root cause A hook failure is the gate doing its job; silencing it ships the bug. Never bypass. ### `gyrum-start-work … --ticket warp#NNN` (warp#1311) The pre-push hook refuses pushes from `feat/* | fix/* | chore/* | docs/* | refactor/*` lacking per-branch metadata under `.gyrum/branch-meta/` (or the audited marker named `branch-meta.no-ticket`) — the structural-vs-documentary lift. If you hit the gate on an in-flight branch, recover by re-creating it via `gyrum-start-work` in a fresh worktree and re-applying your changes. `--no-ticket` is for genuinely-trivial fixes only — pick it explicitly. ### Parse + `cd` to the `WORKTREE:` line (warp#2593) Parse the final `WORKTREE: <path>` (or `WORKTREE-IN-PLACE: <path>`) line of `gyrum-start-work`'s stdout and `cd` to that path before the NEXT Bash call. The interactive-shell auto-cd (warp #459) only fires for shells that have the `gyrum-start-work` shell-function wrapper sourced — non-interactive subshells (Claude Code Bash tool, sub-agents, CI driver scripts) do not. Without this `cd`, every subsequent git operation runs against the operator's canonical checkout — exactly the Rule #2 violation the sibling-clone story exists to prevent. ### Commit-message bodies — one paragraph per line The shared `commit-msg` hook refuses hard-wrapped or over-stuffed paragraphs at author time, so the same lint `gyrum-review-pr` runs over PR-body + commit-messages no longer fires three layers later requiring `git commit --amend` + `git push --force-with-lease` (a path that is sandbox-blocked on agent-created branches per warp#1319). Canonical bypass when the rule genuinely doesn't apply: `git commit --no-verify` — do not add a second escape hatch. See warp#1327 (commit-author-time catch), warp#854 (PR-review-time backstop), ADR-084 (the rule). ### Regression test with every bug fix (warp#1008) PRs closing a `type: bug` ticket are gated by `regression-fixture-for-bug-ticket` (devtools PR #233). The test must fail BEFORE the fix and pass AFTER, and reference the ticket in its name or a `// regression: warp#NNN` comment so reviewers can trace the bug class. Accepted layers: `*_test.go`, `*.test.ts`, `*.spec.ts`, `test_*.py`, `e2e/**/*.spec.ts`. The gate fires on the surface declared in the ticket's `surface:` field (`unit | integration | journey | contract`, default `unit`). This is TDD applied to bug fixes — same shape as red-green-refactor, scaled to where the bug lives. Audited override (use only when the bug genuinely has no testable surface — e.g. visual-only CSS regression with no DOM assertion possible): `gyrum-review-pr --skip-regression-fixture "<reason>"` — logged to `~/.gyrum/admin-overrides.log`. ### Declare `tier` on every public-IP'd server (ADR-175 / warp#1978) PRs touching `gyrum-labs/devtools/infrastructure/server-ids.json`, `ansible/playbooks/install-*.yml`, `ansible/roles/*/tasks/*.yml`, or `**/*.tf` are gated by `trust-boundary`, which runs `scripts/check-trust-boundaries.sh --check` (Phase 3 / warp#1977) in schema-only mode and refuses on gap. Required: `tier: bff | internal | bastion`; for bff/bastion add `tier_justification` (one-liner); for internal add `exposed_ports` (TCP port list) + `trusted_inbound` (alias list). Rationale is BFF + internal-firewalled (one trust boundary per app; internal services trust the network behind it). Audited override (use only when the gap is a documented exception, e.g. a `tier=bastion` addition under separate review): `--skip-trust-boundary "<reason ≥ 10 chars>"` — logged to `~/.gyrum/admin-overrides.log`. See `gyrum-labs/devtools/docs/runbooks/trust-boundary-gate-fail.md` (in devtools) for the per-gap fix table. ### Justify credential-co-tenancy / privilege-escalation (warp#6357) The same `trust-boundary` gate (extended in warp#6357) ALSO refuses any diff that (a) adds a runtime user to `docker`/`sudo`/`wheel` or drops a `NOPASSWD` sudoers fragment, (b) places a credential path (vault/ssh/hcloud/`*token*`) under a runtime user, or (c) adds `privileged: true` / a `/var/run/docker.sock` mount / `cap_add` to a worker container — unless the PR body carries a `## Trust-boundary audit` section (who can reach these creds, blast radius of a compromise, why acceptable). This codifies the mini-64gb root-equivalence finding (internet-fed agents one container-escape from fleet creds) as a deterministic gate. Same audited override: `--skip-trust-boundary "<reason ≥ 10 chars>"`. ### Ship docs alongside script / role / ticket-filing workflow (warp#1981) PRs adding `scripts/<name>.sh` (excluding `*.test.sh`), `ansible/roles/<name>/`, or ticket-filing `.github/workflows/<name>.yml` are gated by `doc-pair`. Scripts need `scripts/README-<name>.md` AND (`docs/HOWTO/<name>.md` OR `docs/runbooks/<name>.md`); roles need `ansible/roles/<name>/README.md`; ticket workflows need `docs/runbooks/<name>.md`. Templates + per-shape guidance in `gyrum-labs/devtools/docs/HOWTO/writing-pair-docs.md` (in devtools). Audited override (use ONLY when the artefact genuinely has no operator-facing surface): `--skip-doc-pair "<reason ≥ 10 chars>"` — logged to `~/.gyrum/admin-overrides.log`. Rationale: documentary "ship docs" rules degrade under pressure; structural refusal at merge time is the only enforcement that holds (same lesson as warp#1311 / warp#1327 / warp#1387 / warp#1008). ### Persona recusal (warp#1392) When a PR carries commits from a fleet persona bot account (`gyrum-priya` / `gyrum-marcus` / `gyrum-lin` / `gyrum-dana` / `gyrum-sasha` / `gyrum-quinn`), `gyrum-review-pr` recuses that persona and drops quorum to 2-of-2 from the remaining default reviewers. When two-or-more default personas (Priya / Marcus / Lin) recuse on the same PR, the gate fails closed and asks the operator to invite a non-default reviewer. Every recusal appends one JSON line to `findings.jsonl` (kind `persona-recusal`) so the decision is auditable. This is the structural enforcement that makes the persona-as-employee architecture (ADR-115) safe — without it a persona could ship a PR and self-approve it the moment dual-role lands. ### Merge-gate decision: approval minimum plus rejection veto (warp#14846) Approval and rejection are separate signals. The 2-of-3 approval quorum is a minimum positive threshold, not permission to erase a negative verdict. `gyrum-review-pr`, its durable auto-merge helper, and `gyrum-complete-pr` each enforce the same exact-head decision: - **At least 2 default personas explicitly `APPROVED` (or 2-of-2 after a recusal) and zero `CHANGES_REQUESTED`** → the clean quorum may proceed. - **Any current-head `CHANGES_REQUESTED` from a required persona** → normal automation is **refused**, even when two other personas approved. Fix the finding and rerun review; completion never dismisses or reinterprets the rejection. - **Empty, `COMMENTED`, malformed, missing, or stale-head evidence** → never increments the approval count. A blank response is not agreement. - **The ≥2-recusal fail-closed rule (persona recusal, above) is unchanged** — the merge gate honours it too. ### Sister-agent collision detection (warp#1511 / warp#1517) `gyrum-start-work` greps open PRs on the target repo for files matching the ticket's likely-touch paths (extracted from the ticket description). Warns on 1-2-file overlap with one open PR (proceeds with stderr note); refuses on >2-file overlap OR (>50% overlap with ≥3 likely-files) unless `--allow-collision "<reason ≥ 10 chars>"` (audited override to `~/.gyrum/start-work-overrides.log` + a finding line); refuses outright on multi-PR overlap with no bypass. The check eliminates the warp#1372/1377 + warp#1373/1378 + warp#1374/1379 duplicate-pair collision pattern. Sibling to the warp#1108 issue-overlap check at the same call-site (issue-overlap catches "another PR mentions this ticket"; file-overlap catches "another PR touches the same files"). ### Assemble dispatch briefs via `gyrum-brief` (warp#1527) The generator pulls the ticket body, parent epic docs[] (warp#1481), the active gate attestation (warp#1420), persona recommendation (warp#1424 / warp#1439), and an open-PR collision check (warp#1517) and emits canonical markdown. Hand-rolled briefs drift between dispatches; substrate-assembled briefs are byte-identical when input is identical, structurally unable to silently miss a gate. Pass `--persona name` to override routing (recorded in provenance); pass `--out path` to write to file. The single command replaces the ~150-line hand-rolled brief operator authored ~12 times/day on 2026-05-06. ### Verify shipped before treating a dep as satisfied (warp#2915) Call `gyrum-verify-shipped warp#NNN` to prove a closing source PR merged before starting dependent source work. Exit 0 in default mode proves the closing PR merged, even when Warp still says `in_progress`: JSON then reports `SOURCE-MERGED` and `delivery_state=pending`. For a delivery dependency or a claim that work is live, use `--require-terminal`; it returns exit 5 while the merged ticket is not Done and exit 0 `SHIPPED` only after Warp reports Done with an exact merge SHA. An older merged PR whose GitHub record omits `mergeCommit` keeps default source-merge success with `merge_sha:null`; terminal mode refuses success without that SHA. A tag, green release build, or merged module does not certify delivery. Unmerged PRs, absent PRs, cancelled/blocked tickets, and API errors retain distinct exits 1/2/3/4. Auto-merge enrollment is not a source merge. ### Dispatch-check before spawning a sub-agent (warp#3710) Run `gyrum-dispatch-check warp#NNN` before invoking `Agent(...)` to spawn a sub-agent on warp#NNN. The verb first validates Warp's canonical actionability projection, then runs four freshness queries (ticket status, merged-PR close-verb, open-PR close-verb, recent main commit). Dispatch only on exit 0, or on exit 5 when the caller deliberately requested an audited freshness bypass for a genuine ship-again case. Exit 1 (already-shipped), 2 (in-progress), 3 (terminal), 4 (recent-main-commit), 6 (usage/API error), and 7 (canonical non-actionable) refuse dispatch. Exit 7 is never bypassable; a Ready item that is canonically non-actionable remains ineligible for `--skip-already-shipped` even when a live claim retains the higher-priority IN-PROGRESS verdict. The bypass audit row lands in `~/.gyrum/admin-overrides.log`. ### Force-push policy (warp#1340) See `gyrum-labs/devtools/policy/git-force-policy.md`. `--force-with-lease` allowed on agent `feat/` / `fix/` / `chore/` branches in `gyrum-start-work` worktrees only; plain `--force` (no-lease) refused anywhere; force-push to `main`/`master` refused with no exception. The harness grounds its push-gating judgment on that file rather than re-deriving the rule per invocation; agents authoring or reviewing a push that needs history rewrite should cite the matching rule number. Recovery when the sandbox blocks a legitimate `--force-with-lease` on an agent branch (warp#1319 / warp#1340 outstanding): non-force `git merge origin/main` fast-forward, NOT `--no-verify` or `--admin`.

Don't file-then-wander. To reclaim a ticket held by another agent on a **fresh, heartbeating** claim there is NO `--steal-from` / live-takeover verb (takeover only fires on a stale lease). Do NOT use the default `gyrum-warp cancel` here: it sends warp#17310's `final: true`, which ENDS the item when the holder releases instead of freeing it for you. Status stays `in_progress`; the holder sees the flag on its next heartbeat (≤5min) and releases. `/reopen` does NOT work here — it only accepts `done`/`cancelled`. 2. Still on the `--handover` path: poll `GET /api/v1/items/{id}` until `claimed_by` clears, then immediately `gyrum-warp claim {id} --force "<reason>"` (add `--allow-sibling-mismatch "<reason ≥30>"` on a sibling-token collision). You're racing the fleet's re-grab — claim in the same tick it frees. **Why:** Operator (jon, 2026-05-25) — a self-filed, locally-verified fix was auto-claimed by a fleet agent that did zero work. `cancel_requested` → holder released on its next heartbeat (~3min) → the claim was won on the poll that saw it go `ready`. Without reserving up front, every file-then-work ticket is a race you can lose. **How to apply:** - Prefer prevention: `reserved_for` at file time for work you'll start now. - Forcing over a still-active claim via `gyrum-complete-pr --admin` needs explicit per-PR operator authorization — the cooperative cancel-and-wait path is the default. - zsh gotcha: `status` is a read-only special var — name the poll-loop variable something else (`st`) or run the loop under `bash -c`. ## Swarm an EPIC — governed activation boosts its children (warp#3051) **Activating a `kind: epic` through `gyrum-warp swarm <epic>` is the "swarm this EPIC" verb:** the command uses the governed `POST /api/v1/items/{id}/activate` lifecycle route and verifies the read-back instead of writing `status` through generic PATCH. The resulting `in_progress` state lifts every open child up one effective-priority tier in the claim and ready queues, so the fleet picks the epic's children ahead of unrelated ready work — without any per-child `reserved_for` cascade. Reserve the EPIC's intent once by activating the parent; the boost follows the parent's status automatically. Reverse it through the governed lifecycle that moves the epic off `in_progress` (`done`/`blocked`). How the boost behaves (server-side, `gyrum-labs/warp/api/internal/items/claim.go` — `epicChildPriorityBoostExpr`, spliced into the claim CTE `claimNextSQL` in `gyrum-labs/warp/api/internal/items/claim_next.go` and the supervisor ready-queue `listWithAffinitySQLTemplate` in `gyrum-labs/warp/api/internal/items/list.go`): - **One tier, never more.** A child of an `in_progress` epic sorts as if one band higher (`low`→`med`, `med`→`high`, `high`→`urgent`), capped at `urgent`; never overflows the band. - **Immediate parent only, in_progress only.** Fires only when the row's direct parent is a `kind: epic` that is `in_progress` and not soft-deleted. `done`/`blocked`/`cancelled`/non-epic parents never boost; top-level tickets never boost. No nesting — an EPIC-of-EPICs does not compound; exactly one tier (v1). - **Anti-starvation: the boost ties, it does not jump.** A boosted `med` child reaches the same effective rank as an unboosted `high` non-child — ties fall through to the `created_at` tiebreak, so a genuinely-higher-priority unrelated ticket is never starved. The boost ranks BELOW the operator `next_up` pin and the `type: bug` elevation, ABOVE `created_at`. - **Claim and ready agree.** The same tier is spliced into both paths, so the row `gyrum-warp ready` SHOWS next is the row a claim would PICK next. **How to apply:** To converge the fleet on an Epic's sub-tickets, run `gyrum-warp swarm <epic>` as a programme owner rather than hand-reserving each child. The command keeps both reads on ordinary `WARP_TOKEN` and uses saved `WARP_APPROVE_TOKEN` (or `WARP_ADMIN_TOKEN` as fallback) only for the activation POST; run `gyrum-warp set-token` if no operator token is saved. It refuses non-Epics and blocked/terminal Epics, treats an already-active Epic as success, and only reports a new activation after Warp's read-back is `in_progress`. Don't reach for the per-child `reserved_for` cascade the boost replaces. The boost honours the priority children already carry — a low-priority swarm won't outrank genuinely urgent independent tickets.

# Screenshot assets This directory holds images referenced by `docs/userguide.md` (and optionally the top-level `README.md`). Hosting them in the repo means they version and diff alongside the code, rather than drifting on an external image host. Every file under `docs/` — including the images — is picked up by `scripts/update-docs.sh` and registered in `docs-viewer/_index.json`, so the viewer can surface them in its sidebar and the validator can confirm links resolve. ## Naming convention Use short, lowercase, hyphen-separated names that describe the **screen** the image shows, not the sequence it appears in: | Good | Avoid | | -------------------------- | ------------------------- | | `tray-idle.png` | `screenshot-1.png` | | `popup-alarm-ready.png` | `fig2.png` | | `settings-empty-state.png` | `img_20260420_153012.png` | Two images of the same screen in different states should share a prefix: `popup-alarm-typing.png` and `popup-alarm-ready.png` make the pair obvious in the sidebar. ## What to capture At minimum, projects with a user-facing UI should include: - The empty-state **and** populated-state of each primary workflow screen. - One completed example of the main output the product produces. - A screenshot for every image referenced from `userguide.md` — an unresolved image link is a broken document in the viewer. Projects with no UI — libraries, CLIs, backend-only services — are exempt from the screenshot requirement; userguide.md can reference terminal output or diagrams instead. ## Capturing Any screenshot tool works. On Ubuntu, GNOME's built-in **Screenshot** (`Shift+PrtSc`) is the easiest. Crop tight to the UI surface being shown; leave a small amount of surrounding context (window chrome, desktop edge) only when the reader needs it to locate the feature. ## After adding or replacing an image Run `scripts/update-docs.sh` to refresh `docs-viewer/_index.json`. A PR that adds an image but forgets the index refresh will fail the `scripts/update-docs.sh --check` gate.

# Method — journey-first UI production Validated against the real ops.gyrum.ai reduction (EPIC warp#14685, Aug 2026). This is the process future products run **from birth**, not after accretion. ## The loop 1. **Evidence before opinions.** Ground the surface list in observed usage + operator priorities. Record evidence sources, window, and gaps _in the ledger_ — a gap you write down is honest; a gap you skip is a lie later. 2. **Journeys first.** Define 5–8 operator journeys (trigger → outcome → screens). Every screen must map to ≥1 journey or become a delete candidate. Weight by stated operator priority; instrument usage later. 3. **IA = the menu is the contract.** One label per destination; zero duplicate seats; detail pages reached by drill-down. Section heads point at hub routes so consolidation keeps reachability. 4. **Reduction is reversible.** Unseat from nav; never delete routes in the same move. Removal of a route needs its own reviewed ticket per clause. 5. **Fix numbers on kept surfaces only** — and make freshness visible (deployed sha + age) so staleness can't ship silently again. 6. **Clause everything.** Every decision enters `docs/products/<product>/clauses.md` as a clause. PRs cite clauses; landing requires merged-PR evidence. ## Mechanical guards that made it work - A **journey↔nav reachability test** (ai-frontend's `journeys-reachability.test.ts`, warp#7943) fails any menu change that strands a journey step. # The runner-fleet mockups Six screens, one live dataset. Each screen shows the same thing in a different arcade language: how big every stage is, and how the work moves through it. The mockups are a direction, not a decision. The clause ledger one directory up records what each screen would have to be true to be worth building. ## What is here | File | What it is | | --- | --- | | `arcade-mockups.html` | the mockup pack: six screens, each with the description and design notes a designer needs | | `arcade-mockups.js` | the drawing code and the live-data binding | | `runner-fleet-infographic.html` | the live dashboard the pack grew out of: 14 views over the same payload | | `runner-fleet-server.py` | the server that holds the credentials and serves the pages | ## Running it The server holds the warp token and the GitHub token; the browser never sees either. It aggregates one payload and serves it to both pages. ```bash python3 runner-fleet-server.py 8137 runner-fleet-infographic.html # the mockup pack: http://127.0.0.1:8137/mockups # the dashboard: http://127.0.0.1:8137/ ``` The server reads `WARP_URL` and `WARP_TOKEN` from `~/.config/gyrum/control-plane.env`, and the fleet's App token from `/tmp/app-token.txt`. It falls back from the App token to the operator token for reads that the App cannot serve. It writes nothing outside its own snapshot and never mutates the fleet. ## The six screens | # | Screen | The idea | | --- | --- | --- | | 01 | The marble run | the pipeline as a wall-mounted marble run; the bucket at the top, a gate opens, the marbles run down; the drum is the test stage | | 02 | The heap | boxes ride belts whose length is the size of their stage, and the finished work piles up in a heap | | 03 | The city | a top-down city; each stage is a district sized by its count, each pull request a resident who walks when their situation changes | | 04 | Pinball board | the pipeline as a pachinko board whose band heights are the stages' sizes | | 05 | Production line | machines down a factory floor, each as tall as its stage, with the work riding the belt | | 06 | Arcade cabinets | a select screen whose cabinets are as tall as their stages, with a preview of the pull requests inside the selected one | ## Two query parameters Both pages read the same live payload and refresh every 25 seconds. - `?only=<id>` — show one screen on its own: `mockups?only=city`, `mockups?only=marble`. The other screens are hidden, so the page is slide-sized. - `?still=1` — paint a bounded number of frames and stop. The animation is continuous by design, which keeps a headless capture waiting forever; the still mode is how a screen gets screenshotted or measured. ## Where the numbers come from One payload, served from `/api/state`: - the **phases** — every pull request bucketed by the state it is in, and the heavy gate's own state on its current head; - the **fleet** — the runner registry: who is registered, who is busy, and which hosts are online; - the **runs** and **jobs** — what the CI lanes are doing; - the **train** — the merge train's own projection of the service order; - the **stats** — throughput, concurrency and the percentiles the fleet publishes. The buckets are derived locally, because the board's phase vocabulary lives in the warp service. The derivation is stated on the dashboard's own delivery page, and the heavy gate's state is read from the heavy workflow's run list rather than from the check rollup — a queued heavy run creates no check run, so the rollup alone would call a pull request green that the heavy gate never ran.

The marble run

A wall-mounted marble run. Everything waiting sits in the bucket at the top; a gate opens and the marbles run down the slope into the next stage.

What this screen shows

One marble per pull request, coloured by the stage it is in. The bucket at the top of the slope is the intake: every pull request that is waiting to be processed sits in it. When a pull request's state changes, its marble leaves the bucket, a gate in the wall opens, and the marble rolls down the track to the collector at the end of the next stage.

The drum in the middle of the run is the test stage: marbles that roll into it are carried around by the paddles and dropped out the other side, which is what being tested feels like. A stage that needs work goes back up the return lift rather than down the slope, and the collector for each stage holds its marbles in a bowl with the count on the sign above it.

Reading it

The height of each stage's bowl is the honest size of that stage: a bowl full of marbles means a stage that is holding a crowd. A marble in flight is a pull request mid-transition.

Design notes

Language
cabinet-style marble run, side elevation
Sprites
glass marbles with a highlight and a soft shadow; steel channel with a double rail; paddle drum; enamel stage signs
Motion
gravity along the channel, constant roll speed, marbles settle into the bowl with a small bounce
Live
one marble per pull request; stage changes drive the motion
02

The heap

Boxes on belts. Each belt is as long as its stage is big, and the finished work piles up in a heap at the end.

What this screen shows

The delivery pipeline as a factory floor. Every pull request is a crate. A crate rides the belt of the stage it is in; the belt is drawn exactly as long as that stage is big, so a stage with eighty pull requests in it is visibly longer than a stage with none. A crate that changes state is lifted to the next belt up.

The heap on the right is the finished work. Crates that reach the last stage are tipped off the end of the belt and fall into the heap, where they settle under their own weight. The heap is the backlog that has been delivered and is still lying about.

Reading it

Long belt = big stage. A crate in the air is a state change in flight. The heap is the pile of work that is finished but not yet cleared away.

Design notes

Language
side-elevation factory line, arcade cabinet palette
Sprites
stencilled crates with a stage stripe; roller belts with a tread pattern; a tipping chute; a settling heap
Motion
belts run at a constant speed; crates hop between belts on a short arc; the heap settles on landing
Live
one crate per pull request; belt length is drawn from the live count
03

The city

A top-down city. Every stage is a district, and every pull request is a resident who walks between districts when their situation changes.

What this screen shows

The fleet as a city seen from above. Each stage is a district, and the district's size is drawn from the number of pull requests in it: a district with many residents has bigger blocks and taller buildings. The residents stand outside the building of their stage, so the crowd outside a building is that stage's backlog, read at a glance.

When a pull request's state changes, its resident walks — out of the district, along the pavement, across the crossing, into the next district. The walk is the change; nothing teleports. The industrial plant in the south-west is the single heavy test slot: it is loaded while a run holds it, and it is the only way onto the heavy lane. The car park in the north-east is the runner pool — one car per runner, and a car leaves the park when its runner picks up work.

Reading it

Residents walking are pull requests mid-transition. A district emptying faster than it fills is work moving forward. Street lights come on at dusk by the real clock.

Design notes

Language
top-down city plan, tile grid, 1990s city-builder palette
Sprites
district blocks with roofs, roof plant and drop shadows; pavement and crossing stripes; residents; cars; street lamps; the plant's chimneys
Motion
residents walk the pavement; cars follow the streets; lamps light at dusk; the plant's smoke drifts
Live
one resident per pull request; block size is drawn from the live count

Pinball board

The pipeline as a pachinko board. Each stage is a band, and a band is as tall as that stage is big.

What this screen shows

A vertical board. The board is cut into seven horizontal bands, one per stage, and the height of each band is drawn from the number of pull requests in that stage — so the board itself is a picture of the shape of the work. A stage with nothing in it is a thin band; the stage holding eighty pull requests is a wide slab of board.

Each pull request is a ball bouncing in its band between the pegs. A ball whose state changes drops through the gate at the bottom of its band into the next one, and the pegs make it scatter on the way down.

Reading it

The band heights are the stage sizes. Balls in flight between two bands are state changes happening. A ball bouncing a lot is a busy stage, not a stuck one.

The panel on the right is the preview: the stage you have selected, the pull requests in it, and the fleet's high score — the throughput the fleet is holding right now. Selecting a cabinet is what the pointer does; nothing here is decoration, every panel is a live number.

Reading it

Cabinet height = stage size. The marquee lamps chase along the selected cabinet. The preview panel lists the actual pull requests in the selected stage.

How these buckets are decided

The board's phase vocabulary lives in the warp service, so these are derived here from what can be measured: the pull request's own state, its check rollup, its review decision, the train's labels, the owning ticket's status, and the heavy gate's own run list — the last one, because the rollup alone cannot see the heavy lane.

About this page

Every pull request, bucketed by how far it has got. The board's own phase vocabulary lives in the warp service, so these buckets are derived here from what can be measured: the pull request's state, its check rollup, its review decision, the train's labels and the owning ticket's status.

Waiting is open, not green and nobody is holding it. Waiting fixed has changes requested or a conflict on the train. In testing has the heavy gate running on its current head. Passed is green and approved, waiting its turn. Waiting for deployment is merged with the delivery tail outstanding. Deployed is merged and delivered within a day; done is merged and settled.

The Heavy column is the one that matters most, and it exists because the check rollup cannot be trusted on its own. The heavy gate is a single-slot workflow that fires only when the train marks its one current candidate ready for review, so it has no check run at all until a runner picks it up, and a pull request whose head moved after that transition never gets one. The light lane is green in seconds, so the rollup reads SUCCESS and the pull request looks tested when it has not been. The column reads the heavy gate's own run list instead: not run means the gate has never run on that head, queued means it is waiting for the single slot, running means it is on a runner now, and failed means the gate ran and went red.

Reading it
the sizes of the first three buckets are the real signal: a long "waiting" bucket means the fleet is not picking work up, and a "passed" bucket full of not run means the gate has not been reached rather than that the work is sound

# The queue, from waiting to deployed How a pull request actually travels from "somebody opened it" to "it is delivered and settled" in `gyrum-labs/devtools`, what each stage means, what moves a pull request out of it, and the ways it gets stuck. Everything here was measured against the running fleet on 2026-11-06. The stages the board shows are the board's own phase vocabulary. They are **derived**, because the phase lives in the warp service and the board reads what it can see. Two of the derivations are wrong in a way that matters, and both are called out below. --- ## Before the queue A pull request exists: open, on a branch, usually a draft at first. Nothing has happened to it yet. It carries no train labels, so it is not in the service order and no lane is waiting on it. The light CI lane (`ci-light`) runs on every push — it is four jobs (triage, shellcheck, smoke, changed-tests) and it is independent of the heavy lane, so it never queues behind anything. ## 1. waiting *Open, not green, nobody holding changes.* The pull request is in the fleet but not yet in the train's service order. It usually arrives here because it was opened, or because it was re-pushed and the previous checks went stale. **What it needs to leave:** - the light lane green (usually seconds), and - a review quorum — the persona panel's two formal approvals on the **exact head**. **What the fleet does here:** the train's feeder looks for a claimable pull request — one that is reviewable, green, and not conflicted — and enqueues it. That is the `train:queued` label, and it puts the pull request in the service order at the back. **How it gets stuck here:** a pull request can sit in `waiting` for weeks without anything being wrong with it. The pile's own report (106 pull requests, read on 2026-11-06) put 36 of them in a "review evidence" family — the train refused their review evidence, so they need a re-review, not a re-run. 27 of the 35 re-land candidates wanted exactly that. ## 2. waiting fixed *Changes requested, or a conflict with the train.* The review panel asked for changes, or the pull request conflicts with what the train is serving. **What happens here:** the pull request leaves the service order (it is dequeued, with an audited reason) and the author works on it. When the fix is pushed, the **head moves**, and that has two consequences that are easy to miss: - the approvals that were given for the old head are now stale — the evidence is bound to the head it was signed for, so the pull request needs a re-review; - the heavy gate has never run on the new head, so it needs a heavy run as well. **How it gets stuck here:** if the head moves *again* while the review is in flight, the reviewer may be reading a commit that is no longer the head. That is not a hypothetical — on 2026-11-06 the head of the queue had a changes-request written against `ae210cd1` while the head was already `e71c0064`, and the pull request sat approved-but-refused until the review was redone. ## 3. in testing *The heavy gate, on the exact head.* This is the only stage where the heavy lane is involved, and it is where the queue's real bottleneck lives. **How the heavy gate starts.** The heavy workflow (`ci.yml`) fires on the pull request's `ready_for_review` event. The train therefore flips its candidate to a draft and back to ready — that transition is what emits the event. Until 2026-11-07 that transition was being refused by the fleet's own `gh` policy wrapper, because the train's sanctioned marker was inherited from whatever launched the worker rather than carried at the call. The result was `ready-transition-failed`: the heavy gate was never asked to run for a train candidate at all. That is fixed in [warp#22457](https://warp.gyrum.ai/items/22457). **The shape of one heavy run:** | Step | What it does | |---|---| | triage | reads the diff shape; picks the lane | | plan | lists the test units and partitions them into shards | | build-vet | builds and vets the toolchain | | **shards** | the test units, partitioned (`shard 1 of N`) — one runner per shard, in parallel | | frontend-evidence / capture | captures the frontend evidence; needs the network | | aggregates | `structural-checks` and the rollup | **The lane is one run at a time.** Every heavy run in the repository shares a single concurrency group (`ci-devtools`), deliberately (warp#17523): the merge train is the admission authority, so a candidate validates against current `main`, merges, and gives push-`main` its turn before another candidate can consume the pool. The cost is that the fleet's fifteen runners are idle whenever the lane is not running, and that one long-held lane starves every other pull request. **How it gets stuck here:** three ways, all measured. - A run for a **superseded head** sits in the lane and can never produce a usable result. On 2026-11-06 one such run held the lane from 20:09 to 21:40 while the lane ran no other work. The canceller that should have removed it could not see it: it inventoried only `event=pull_request` runs, while the train's dispatched runs are `event=workflow_dispatch` (warp#22443). - The **pin-advance bot's own pull request** takes the lane hourly and fails every time. - A shard that **times out** is classified `INFRA-KILL` — rerun-eligible, not a real failure — but the run is still red until someone re-runs it. ## 4. passed *Green and approved; the train may merge it.* The heavy gate is green on the exact head, the panel's quorum is signed for that same head, and the pull request is mergeable. It is now waiting for the train's turn, not for anything to be built. **What happens here:** the train merges it, subject to its own gates — clean merge, no conflict, the merge is the train's, not an operator's. **How it gets stuck here:** the head can move under the pull request at any point (a re-trigger commit, an operator push), and a moved head invalidates both the review quorum and the heavy run. The pull request goes back to `waiting fixed` or `in testing` and the cycle repeats. ## 5. waiting for deployment *Merged; the delivery tail is not finished.* The code is in `main`. What is left is the **delivery tail**: the owning warp ticket has to reach `done`, because the ticket is where the work was tracked from the start. This is where the pile looks alarming — 80 pull requests on the board — and where the board was lying: > The 80 were not "deploying". 67 of their tickets are **already closed**; the board read their > status as unknown because the ticket lookup was scoped to one repository, and a ticket lives in > the repository it was filed against — which for most of these is `dark-factory` or > `ai-research`, not `devtools`. With the lookup fixed, those pull requests belong in `done`. The real remainder is small: pull requests whose ticket still says `awaiting_merge` (the ticket never moved on after the merge) or `ready`. **How it gets stuck here:** a ticket that is closed but whose pull request is still open, or a ticket that is waiting for the merge that already happened. Both are cheap to fix and both make the queue look far worse than it is. ## 6. deployed *Merged, ticket done, less than 24 hours ago.* The delivery tail finished. The pull request is settled but still recent, so it stays visible as `deployed` for a day. ## 7. done *Merged, ticket done, more than 24 hours ago.* Settled. Nothing is owed. --- ## How the stages are derived | Stage | Rule | |---|---| | waiting | open · checks not green · review not `CHANGES_REQUESTED` | | waiting fixed | `reviewDecision = CHANGES_REQUESTED`, or label `train:conflict` | | in testing | the heavy gate has a run on the pull request's **current head** — queued or running — or the check rollup is `PENDING` | | passed | open · rollup `SUCCESS` · review `APPROVED` | | waiting for deployment | merged · owning ticket not done | | deployed | merged · ticket done · merged less than 24h ago | | done | merged · ticket done · merged more than 24h ago | **Two corrections to the derivation, both made on 2026-11-06:** 1. **`in testing` must not be read from the check rollup.** A queued heavy run creates no check run at all, so the rollup reports `SUCCESS` from the light lane alone. Reading the heavy gate's own run list is the only honest signal. Before the fix, 48 of the 49 pull requests in `passed` had never been through the heavy gate on their current head. 2. **The ticket's status must be resolved by ticket number, across repositories.** A repo-scoped lookup cannot see a ticket filed against another repo, and every such pull request reads as un-delivered forever. ## What to look at when the queue is stuck | Symptom | Where to look | |---|---| | Many pull requests, nothing running | Is the heavy lane occupied? `gyrum-merge-train status` names the head; the lane's holder is in the Actions list. | | The head is approved but will not merge | Does the head have a heavy run? A `ready-transition-failed` in the train worker's log means the gate was never asked to run. | | A pull request is stuck in `waiting` | Read the train's own drop reason on the pull request, not the phase: the pile tool (`gyrum-devtools merge-train-pile --repo gyrum-labs/devtools`) sorts every dropped pull request into re-land / rework / close / decide with the evidence. | | `passed` looks full of untested work | Read the Heavy column. `not run` means the heavy gate never ran on that head — the pull request is not tested, whatever the rollup says. | | A run is red but nothing is wrong with the code | Check the classification: `INFRA-KILL` (a timeout) and `INFRA-INCOMPLETE` (exit 75, a missing artifact) are rerun-eligible, not real failures. |

# Runbook — `scripts/update-docs.sh` reports drift When CI (or a local `scripts/update-docs.sh --check`) fails with a drift report, a file under `docs/shared/` no longer matches its canonical source in `~/.gyrum/devtools/docs/shared/`. This runbook is the recovery procedure. ## Symptom ``` $ scripts/update-docs.sh --check update-docs: docs/shared/gate-stack.md differs from source — re-run without --check ``` `--check` exits non-zero; the PR's structural checks go red. ## Cause `docs/shared/*` files are generated, not authored. Drift happens when: 1. Someone hand-edited a `docs/shared/` file (forbidden — the header says so), or 2. The canonical source in `gyrum-labs/devtools` advanced and this repo hasn't re-run the generator since. ## Fix ```sh # 1. Make sure the deployed devtools checkout is current. git -C ~/.gyrum/devtools pull --ff-only # 2. Regenerate the shared docs in this repo. scripts/update-docs.sh # 3. Confirm the drift is gone. scripts/update-docs.sh --check # exits 0 # 4. Commit the regenerated files. git add docs/shared docs-viewer/_index.json git commit -m "docs: refresh shared docs from devtools" ``` If step 3 still reports drift after a clean regenerate, the source file itself was edited in this repo's history — restore it from devtools by re-running step 2 and discarding any local edits to `docs/shared/`. ## Never - **Never** edit a `docs/shared/` file directly to silence the check — the next regenerate overwrites it and the drift returns. - **Never** delete the `AUTO-GENERATED` header; the `--check` gate keys on it to tell a generated file from an authored one.

Letting each project write its own version of those explanations sounds harmless at first, but it drifts. A paragraph gets copied into a new repo, the original is updated, and six months later the copy is subtly wrong in ways that only reveal themselves when someone joins the team and believes the stale version. Centralising the shared content fixes that at the source: there is exactly one file per topic, the canonical one lives here, and every consuming repo reads from the same place. The criterion for putting a file here is therefore strict — the content must be valuable in every project and identical across all of them. Documents that describe a particular repository's architecture or domain model stay in that repository; they are not shared truth. ## How the content reaches consumers The delivery mechanism is `scripts/update-docs.sh`, a thin wrapper `gyrum-setup` drops into every consuming project. Running it copies the files in this directory into the project's own `docs/shared/` with an `AUTO-GENERATED` header pointing back to source, and regenerates `docs-viewer/_index.json` so the sidebar reflects what actually lives under `docs/`. The copy is one-way and periodic: consumers re-run the script to pick up updates, so edits to a file in this directory propagate only on the next refresh in each consuming repo. Dana in particular is the reviewer to watch for documentation edits, because her remit is reader onboarding and explanatory prose; her advisory verdict gates the local review script even though it does not count toward GitHub's formal approval threshold. The viewer-validator (see `gate-stack.md`) runs before the panel and blocks on any structural violation of `doc-standards.md`, so edits here must themselves conform to the contract. An AI review panel reads the diff before a human does. Contract tests validate that each service's HTTP surface still matches the OpenAPI spec it promises. Fleet end-to-end tests drive real browsers against real composed services and catch the integration bugs that only exist when the pieces are wired together. This document is the single authoritative description of all four layers — what each one catches, what it misses, how to run it, and how to decide which layer a new test belongs in. The document exists because a real bug recently passed every layer we had at the time and was only caught when a human loaded the browser. A playbook runtime that should have substituted `${inputs.X}` did not; the unit tests did not exercise the substitution path, the AI panel approved the diff, and contract tests for the playbook runtime did not yet exist. The browser-level failure was not a freak event — it was the predictable consequence of not having written down which bugs each layer is responsible for. Writing it down, and telling every engineer where to add the next test, is the fix. ## Overview — the four layers ```mermaid flowchart TB Push[git push] --> L1[Layer 1 — Pre-push hooks] L1 -->|green| PR[Pull request opened] PR --> L2[Layer 2 — 3-persona AI review] PR --> L3[Layer 3 — Contract tests] L2 -->|2 of 3 approvals + Dana| Merge{Branch protection} L3 -->|green| Merge Merge -->|merged to main| L4[Layer 4 — Fleet E2E] L4 -->|scheduled + manual| Monitor[Production monitoring] ``` | Layer | Runs | Speed | Blast radius | What it catches | |-------|------|-------|--------------|-----------------| | 1. Pre-push hooks | Every `git push` | ~15s | Single repo | Compile, lint, unit tests, complexity, coverage, secrets, file size | | 2. 3-persona AI review | Every PR | ~90s | Single repo | Architecture drift, security holes, TDD discipline, Go idioms | | 3. Contract tests | CI per PR | ~30s | Service API | Response-shape drift, status codes, required fields | | 4. Fleet E2E | CI scheduled + manual | ~5min | Cross-service | Integration bugs, SSR quirks, CORS, cross-repo deploys | The layers are ordered by cost and by the scope of the failure each one can see. Layer 1 is cheap, runs on every push, and only sees the single repo. Layer 4 is expensive, runs on a schedule, and sees every service in the fleet at once. A bug that only shows up when two services talk to each other will never be caught by layer 1, no matter how thorough the unit tests are; a bug in a pure function will be caught by layer 1 long before layer 4 gets anywhere near it. Each layer is there because the layers above it cannot catch what it catches, and running any subset of them without the others leaves a class of bug uncovered. The rest of this document walks the layers in order, explains what each one can and cannot see, and finishes with a decision table for picking the right layer when you are writing a new test. ## Layer 1 — Pre-push hooks The first layer is a set of fast mechanical checks that run on every `git push` through the `pre-push` hook that `gyrum-setup` installs. A cheap subset — build and test — runs locally on the developer's laptop before the push leaves the machine, so obviously broken commits are caught before anyone else sees them. The full suite (linters, coverage, secret scans, complexity limits, security scanners) runs inside `gyrum-review-pr` and is what the gate actually enforces. The split is deliberate: the hook stays fast enough that nobody is tempted to bypass it, and the expensive checks run once, at review time, where their output is read. ### What it catches This layer is deliberately mechanical. It only asks questions that have objective answers — *did the build succeed?*, *are there any secrets in the diff?*, *is this new file under the file-size threshold?* — and it refuses to compromise on them. If it passes, you know the code builds and runs its tests, which is the floor below which nothing merges. <!-- consumer may not have .gyrum/debt-thresholds.json yet — overridable per-project, optional --> <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> The [`gate-stack.md`](./gate-stack.md) document is the authoritative list of every check that runs in this layer and whether it is blocking or warn-level.
